claim: A novel variant c.269A>C in UBQLN4 was identified in a familial ALS case.
source: This variant, c.269A>C, was located in exon 3, leading to the change of aspartate to alanine, p.D90A at the protein level (Figure 1C).
evidence: The variant was identified through sequencing of familial ALS cases and confirmed by sequencing chromatograms shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The UBQLN4 variant c.269A>C results in the amino acid change p.D90A.
source: This variant, c.269A>C, was located in exon 3, leading to the change of aspartate to alanine, p.D90A at the protein level (Figure 1C).
evidence: The protein-level consequence is directly stated and shown in sequencing data.

claim: The female patient (III3) with the UBQLN4D90A variant had disease onset at 55 years with disease duration of two years.
source: The female patient (III3) with this UBQLN4D90A variant had an age of disease onset at 55 years, with disease duration of two years.
evidence: Clinical information about the patient is directly stated in the manuscript.

claim: The patient's mother (II3), maternal aunt (II2), and maternal cousin (III1) also developed ALS.
source: Her mother (II3), maternal aunt (II2) and a maternal cousin (III1) also developed ALS and died of respiratory failure two to five years following disease onset.
evidence: Family history is documented in the text and shown in the pedigree.

claim: The UBQLN4 variant was not present in 332 in-house controls.
source: The variant was neither present in our 332 in-house controls, nor in any SNP databases with a total of >15,000 sequenced alleles nor in the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) database in a total of 60,706 unrelated individuals.
evidence: The absence of the variant in control populations is explicitly stated.

claim: The UBQLN4 variant was not present in SNP databases with >15,000 sequenced alleles.
source: The variant was neither present in our 332 in-house controls, nor in any SNP databases with a total of >15,000 sequenced alleles nor in the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) database in a total of 60,706 unrelated individuals.
evidence: The absence in SNP databases is explicitly stated.

claim: The UBQLN4 variant was not present in the ExAC database containing 60,706 unrelated individuals.
source: The variant was neither present in our 332 in-house controls, nor in any SNP databases with a total of >15,000 sequenced alleles nor in the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) database in a total of 60,706 unrelated individuals.
evidence: The absence in ExAC database is explicitly stated.

claim: The amino acid D90 is adjacent to the UBL domain of UBQLN4.
source: The amino acid D90 is adjacent to the UBL domain of UBQLN4 (Figure 1B) and is highly conserved during evolution, suggesting its importance in structural and functional properties of the protein.
evidence: The position is stated in text and shown in the domain diagram in Figure 1B.

claim: The amino acid D90 is highly conserved during evolution.
source: The amino acid D90 is adjacent to the UBL domain of UBQLN4 (Figure 1B) and is highly conserved during evolution, suggesting its importance in structural and functional properties of the protein.
evidence: Conservation is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells showed a significant increase in total number of neurites compared to cells expressing wild-type UBQLN4.
source: UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells showed a significant increase in the total number of neurites as compared to cells expressing wild-type UBQLN4, or non-transfected cells (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 2C demonstrates statistical significance (p<0.0001).

claim: UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells showed a significant increase in total number of neurites compared to non-transfected cells.
source: UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells showed a significant increase in the total number of neurites as compared to cells expressing wild-type UBQLN4, or non-transfected cells (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 2C demonstrates statistical significance (p<0.0001).

claim: Abnormal motor axon branching was observed in UBQLN4D90A-injected zebrafish embryos but not in UBQLN4-WT or uninjected embryos.
source: When mRNAs encoding UBQLN4-WT or UBQLN4D90A were injected into zebrafish embryos, we observed abnormal motor axon branching in UBQLN4D90A but not UBQLN4-WT or uninjected embryos (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: Observations are documented in text and quantified in Figure 2D showing statistical significance.

claim: UBQLN4-WT and UBQLN4D90A-injected fish embryos developed normally without gross morphological abnormalities.
source: Both UBQLN4-WT and UBQLN4D90A-injected fish embryos otherwise developed normally and showed neither gross morphological abnormalities nor significant changes in motor axon length, suggesting specificity of the motor axon branching phenotype.
evidence: Normal development is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: UBQLN4-WT and UBQLN4D90A-injected fish embryos showed no significant changes in motor axon length.
source: Both UBQLN4-WT and UBQLN4D90A-injected fish embryos otherwise developed normally and showed neither gross morphological abnormalities nor significant changes in motor axon length, suggesting specificity of the motor axon branching phenotype.
evidence: Lack of motor axon length changes is explicitly stated.

claim: Expression levels of UBQLN4-WT and UBQLN4D90A were comparable in all experiments.
source: In all experiments, expression levels of UBQLN4-WT and UBQLN4D90A were comparable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Comparable expression is stated and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: UBQLN4D90A expression resulted in reduced protein turnover as indicated by significantly greater GFP signal compared to UBQLN4-WT.
source: UBQLN4D90A expression resulted in reduced protein turnover, as indicated by significantly greater GFP signal compared to UBQLN4-WT or UbG76V-GFP alone (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 3B shows statistically significant differences in GFP levels.

claim: Cells transfected with UbG76V-GFP + UBQLN4D90A showed much less GFP degradation in cycloheximide assay, indicating impairment of proteasomal function.
source: Cells transfected with UbG76V-GFP + UBQLN4D90A showed much less GFP degradation, indicating impairment of proteasomal function by the ALS-associated UBQLN4D90A variant (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Cycloheximide assay results shown in Figure 3C,D demonstrate reduced degradation over time.

claim: There was a significant decrease in beta-catenin in UBQLN4-WT-expressing cells compared to non-transfected cells.
source: There was a significant decrease in beta-catenin in UBQLN4-WT-expressing cells compared to non-transfected cells, suggesting a role for UBQLN4 in facilitating beta-catenin degradation.
evidence: Western blot quantification in Figure 3E,F shows statistically significant differences.

claim: A significant increase of beta-catenin was detected in UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells compared to those expressing UBQLN4-WT.
source: Moreover, we detected a significant increase of beta-catenin in UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells compared to those expressing UBQLN4-WT, suggesting that the UBQLN4D90A mutation disrupts beta-catenin degradation (Figure 3F).
evidence: Western blot quantification in Figure 3F shows statistically significant differences.

claim: Nuclear beta-catenin accumulation was confirmed in UBQLN4D90A-expressing primary mouse spinal motor neurons.
source: Immunostaining in primary mouse spinal motor neurons validated these observations, and further confirmed nuclear beta-catenin accumulation in UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Immunostaining and quantification in Figure 3G,H demonstrate increased nuclear localization.

claim: Treatment with 0.1 μM quercetin reduced nuclear accumulation of beta-catenin in UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells.
source: Immunostaining for beta-catenin in mouse spinal motor neurons transfected with UBQLN4-WT or UBQLN4D90A revealed significantly greater nuclear accumulation of beta-catenin in UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells as compared to UBQLN4-WT-expressing cells (Figure 4A,B). This accumulation was reduced by treatment with 0.1 μM quercetin, confirming the inhibitor's effectiveness.
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4B shows rescue of nuclear beta-catenin localization with quercetin treatment.

claim: The total number of neurites in 0.1 μM quercetin-treated UBQLN4D90A-expressing neurons was rescued to wild-type levels.
source: Indeed, the total number of neurites in 0.1 μM quercetin-treated UBQLN4D90A-expressing neurons was rescued to wild-type levels (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4D shows statistical rescue of neurite number with quercetin treatment.

claim: The percentage of motor axons with aberrant branching morphology in 50 μM quercetin-treated UBQLN4D90A-expressing zebrafish embryos was significantly reduced compared to vehicle-treated embryos.
source: Moreover, the percentage of motor axons with aberrant branching morphology in 50 μM quercetin-treated UBQLN4D90A-expressing zebrafish embryos was significantly reduced as compared to vehicle-treated embryos (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4F shows statistical rescue of aberrant branching with quercetin treatment.

claim: 267 familial ALS index cases and 411 sporadic ALS cases were sequenced for UBQLN4 variants.
source: We examined 267 familial ALS index cases and 411 sporadic ALS cases, and identified a variant in a familial ALS case (Figure 1A).
evidence: The number of cases examined is explicitly stated.

claim: Ubiquilins recognize and bind polyubiquitinated substrate proteins through a C-terminal ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain.
source: The best understood function of ubiquilins is in the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), where they recognize and bind polyubiquitinated substrate proteins through a C-terminal ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain and deliver them to the proteasome through an N-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain (Marín, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marín, 2014.

claim: Ubiquilins deliver polyubiquitinated substrates to the proteasome through an N-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain.
source: The best understood function of ubiquilins is in the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), where they recognize and bind polyubiquitinated substrate proteins through a C-terminal ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain and deliver them to the proteasome through an N-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain (Marín, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marín, 2014.

claim: Additional roles for ubiquilins in autophagy and ER-associated degradation have been described.
source: Additional roles for ubiquilins in autophagy and ER-associated degradation have also been described (Hjerpe et al., 2016; Lee and Brown, 2012; Lim et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The UPS and autophagy are indispensible for multiple aspects of neuronal development.
source: The UPS and autophagy are indispensible for multiple aspects of neuronal development (Cecconi and Levine, 2008; Hamilton and Zito, 2013) and are crucial in maintaining homeostasis in the aging nervous system (Groen and Gillingwater, 2015; Rezania and Roos, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The UPS and autophagy are crucial in maintaining homeostasis in the aging nervous system.
source: The UPS and autophagy are indispensible for multiple aspects of neuronal development (Cecconi and Levine, 2008; Hamilton and Zito, 2013) and are crucial in maintaining homeostasis in the aging nervous system (Groen and Gillingwater, 2015; Rezania and Roos, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dysfunction of UPS and autophagy pathways contributes to neurodegenerative diseases characterized by protein aggregation.
source: Dysfunction of these pathways contributes to neurodegenerative diseases characterized by protein aggregation (Huang et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Variants in UBQLN1 and UBQLN2 have been linked to neurological disorders.
source: Accordingly, variants in UBQLN1 and UBQLN2 have been linked to neurological disorders.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations in the text.

claim: Ubiquilin1 protein has been associated with neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease.
source: The ubiquilin1 protein, encoded by UBQLN1, has been associated with neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is proposed to contribute to protein aggregates characteristic of AD pathology (El Ayadi et al., 2012; Mah et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to El Ayadi et al., 2012 and Mah et al., 2000.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms in UBQLN1 were suggested to confer susceptibility to Alzheimer's disease.
source: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms in UBQLN1 were suggested to confer susceptibility to Alzheimer's disease (Bertram et al., 2005; Kamboh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bertram et al., 2005 and Kamboh et al., 2006.

claim: Mutations in UBQLN2 have been related to familial X-linked ALS/FTD.
source: Mutations in UBQLN2 have been related to familial X-linked ALS/FTD (Deng et al., 2011) and heterogeneous X-linked dominant neurodegeneration (Fahed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in UBQLN2 have been related to heterogeneous X-linked dominant neurodegeneration.
source: Mutations in UBQLN2 have been related to familial X-linked ALS/FTD (Deng et al., 2011) and heterogeneous X-linked dominant neurodegeneration (Fahed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fahed et al., 2014.

claim: A variant E54D in UBQLN1 has been reported in a single patient with atypical motor neuron disease consistent with Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome.
source: A variant, E54D, in UBQLN1 has been reported in a single patient with atypical motor neuron disease consistent with Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome (González-Pérez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to González-Pérez et al., 2012.

claim: UBQLN4 is widely expressed and shows substantial homology to human UBQLN2.
source: UBQLN4, like UBQLN1 and UBQLN2, is widely expressed and shows substantial homology to human UBQLN2 (Marín, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marín, 2014.

claim: The UbG76V-GFP fusion protein serves as a reporter for UPS function.
source: We used the UbG76V-GFP fusion protein as a reporter for UPS function (Dantuma et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dantuma et al., 2000.

claim: The G76V substitution produces an uncleavable ubiquitin moiety that acts as a proteasome degradation signal.
source: The G76V substitution produces an uncleavable ubiquitin moiety that acts as a proteasome degradation signal, thereby targeting GFP for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the UbG76V-GFP reporter system.

claim: Loss of UBA1 was shown to cause motor axon abnormalities similar to those observed with UBQLN4D90A.
source: Recently, loss of the ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 1 (UBA1) was shown to cause motor axon abnormalities similar to what we observed. In the UBA1 study, the phenotypes were shown to result from heightened beta-catenin signaling, caused by loss of Uba1 and dysfunction of ubiquitination pathways (Wishart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wishart et al., 2014.

claim: Quercetin acts by restricting beta-catenin nuclear localization to reduce beta-catenin-dependent signaling.
source: To address this possibility we utilized quercetin, which acts by restricting beta-catenin nuclear localization to reduce beta-catenin-dependent signaling (Park et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2005.

claim: The degradation of beta-catenin is known to be carried out through the ubiquitin proteasome pathway.
source: The degradation of beta-catenin is known to be carried out through the ubiquitin proteasome pathway (Aberle et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aberle et al., 1997.

claim: Beta-catenin-dependent signaling plays a critical role in regulating multiple aspects of neuronal development, including neurite outgrowth.
source: Beta-catenin-dependent signaling has been shown to play a critical role in regulating multiple aspects of neuronal development, including neurite outgrowth (Votin et al., 2005), axon guidance (Avilés and Stoeckli, 2016; Maro et al., 2009), and target innervation (Salinas and Zou, 2008; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Votin et al., 2005.

claim: Beta-catenin-dependent signaling plays a critical role in regulating axon guidance.
source: Beta-catenin-dependent signaling has been shown to play a critical role in regulating multiple aspects of neuronal development, including neurite outgrowth (Votin et al., 2005), axon guidance (Avilés and Stoeckli, 2016; Maro et al., 2009), and target innervation (Salinas and Zou, 2008; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Avilés and Stoeckli, 2016 and Maro et al., 2009.

claim: Beta-catenin-dependent signaling plays a critical role in regulating target innervation.
source: Beta-catenin-dependent signaling has been shown to play a critical role in regulating multiple aspects of neuronal development, including neurite outgrowth (Votin et al., 2005), axon guidance (Avilés and Stoeckli, 2016; Maro et al., 2009), and target innervation (Salinas and Zou, 2008; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Salinas and Zou, 2008 and Wu et al., 2012.

claim: Aberrant motor axon morphology has been associated with ALS-related genes including TDP-43.
source: This is consistent with reports of aberrant motor axon morphology associated with ALS-related genes including TDP-43 (Kabashi et al., 2010), SOD1 (Clark et al., 2016; Lemmens et al., 2007; Ramesh et al., 2010) and C9orf72 (Burguete et al., 2015; Ciura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kabashi et al., 2010.

claim: Aberrant motor axon morphology has been associated with ALS-related gene SOD1.
source: This is consistent with reports of aberrant motor axon morphology associated with ALS-related genes including TDP-43 (Kabashi et al., 2010), SOD1 (Clark et al., 2016; Lemmens et al., 2007; Ramesh et al., 2010) and C9orf72 (Burguete et al., 2015; Ciura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2016; Lemmens et al., 2007; and Ramesh et al., 2010.

claim: Aberrant motor axon morphology has been associated with ALS-related gene C9orf72.
source: This is consistent with reports of aberrant motor axon morphology associated with ALS-related genes including TDP-43 (Kabashi et al., 2010), SOD1 (Clark et al., 2016; Lemmens et al., 2007; Ramesh et al., 2010) and C9orf72 (Burguete et al., 2015; Ciura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burguete et al., 2015 and Ciura et al., 2013.

claim: The ALS-associated UBQLN4 variant impairs proteasomal function.
source: We further demonstrate that the ALS-associated UBQLN4 variant impairs proteasomal function, and identify the Wnt signaling pathway effector beta-catenin as a UBQLN4 substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated through UbG76V-GFP reporter assays and cycloheximide stability assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Beta-catenin is a UBQLN4 substrate.
source: We further demonstrate that the ALS-associated UBQLN4 variant impairs proteasomal function, and identify the Wnt signaling pathway effector beta-catenin as a UBQLN4 substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the observation that UBQLN4-WT expression reduces beta-catenin levels while UBQLN4D90A expression leads to beta-catenin accumulation.

claim: Inhibition of beta-catenin function rescues the UBQLN4 variant-induced motor axon phenotypes.
source: Inhibition of beta-catenin function rescues the UBQLN4 variant-induced motor axon phenotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quercetin treatment experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ALS-associated variant in UBQLN4 regulates motor axon morphogenesis.
source: A novel ALS-associated variant in UBQLN4 regulates motor axon morphogenesis
evidence: This is the title claim supported by all experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The conservation of amino acid D90 suggests its importance in structural and functional properties of UBQLN4.
source: The amino acid D90 is adjacent to the UBL domain of UBQLN4 (Figure 1B) and is highly conserved during evolution, suggesting its importance in structural and functional properties of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary conservation data.

claim: The ALS-associated UBQLN4 variant interferes with normal motor axon morphogenesis in culture and in vivo.
source: These results indicate that the ALS-associated UBQLN4 variant interferes with normal motor axon morphogenesis in culture and in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental results in primary neurons and zebrafish.

claim: UBQLN4 plays a role in facilitating beta-catenin degradation.
source: There was a significant decrease in beta-catenin in UBQLN4-WT-expressing cells compared to non-transfected cells, suggesting a role for UBQLN4 in facilitating beta-catenin degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UBQLN4-WT expression reduces beta-catenin levels.

claim: The UBQLN4D90A mutation disrupts beta-catenin degradation.
source: Moreover, we detected a significant increase of beta-catenin in UBQLN4D90A-expressing cells compared to those expressing UBQLN4-WT, suggesting that the UBQLN4D90A mutation disrupts beta-catenin degradation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UBQLN4D90A expression leads to beta-catenin accumulation.

claim: Motor axon morphogenesis phenotypes characteristic of UBQLN4D90A expression may result from beta-catenin accumulation.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that motor axon morphogenesis phenotypes characteristic of UBQLN4D90A expression may result from beta-catenin accumulation, and that inhibition of beta-catenin is sufficient to mitigate UBQLN4D90A variant-induced phenotypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with quercetin.

claim: Inhibition of beta-catenin is sufficient to mitigate UBQLN4D90A variant-induced phenotypes.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that motor axon morphogenesis phenotypes characteristic of UBQLN4D90A expression may result from beta-catenin accumulation, and that inhibition of beta-catenin is sufficient to mitigate UBQLN4D90A variant-induced phenotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quercetin rescue experiments.

claim: The D90A mutation lies near the UBL domain of UBQLN4.
source: Because the D90A mutation lies near the UBL domain, the UBQLN4D90A variant may compromise interaction with proteasomes, consistent with our finding of proteasomal impairment in UBQLN4D90A-expressing neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The UBQLN4D90A variant may compromise interaction with proteasomes.
source: Because the D90A mutation lies near the UBL domain, the UBQLN4D90A variant may compromise interaction with proteasomes, consistent with our finding of proteasomal impairment in UBQLN4D90A-expressing neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of the mutation and the observed proteasomal impairment.

claim: UBQLN4D90A expression may affect motor neuron development through dysregulated beta-catenin-dependent signaling.
source: Therefore UBQLN4D90A expression, which compromises UPS function and causes beta-catenin accumulation, may affect motor neuron development through dysregulated beta-catenin-dependent signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed effects on UPS function, beta-catenin levels, and motor axon morphology.

claim: Defects in motor axon morphogenesis may confer functional vulnerability at later stages, rendering motor neurons susceptible to degeneration in ALS.
source: Early neurodevelopmental processes affect mature neuron functions; motor axon morphogenesis is essential for action potential transmission and target innervation. Defects in these processes may therefore confer functional vulnerability at later stages, rendering motor neurons susceptible to degeneration in ALS.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about how developmental defects might contribute to later neurodegeneration.

claim: The UBQLN4D90A variant acts in a dominant-negative manner.
source: Our observation that UBQLN4D90A expression impairs proteasome function (Figure 3A–D) suggests that the variant acts in a dominant-negative manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteasome impairment data.

claim: The UBQLN4D90A variant results in a partial loss-of-function.
source: However, our finding that beta-catenin level was still reduced in UBQLN4D90A expressing cells compared to nontransfected cells (Figure 3E,F) suggests that the variant results in a partial loss-of-function.
evidence: This is inferred from the beta-catenin level data.

claim: In the short term UBQLN4D90A functions with reduced efficiency but still facilitates degradation of substrates.
source: This may be because in the short term UBQLN4D90A functions with reduced efficiency, but still facilitates degradation of substrates.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain the partial loss-of-function observation.

claim: Reduced UBQLN4 functional efficiency may overload the proteasome pathway over time.
source: Overtime, reduced UBQLN4 functional efficiency may overload the proteasome pathway; therefore, an initial partial loss of function can eventually lead to a dominant negative gain of function outcome.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about long-term consequences.

claim: An initial partial loss of function can eventually lead to a dominant negative gain of function outcome.
source: Overtime, reduced UBQLN4 functional efficiency may overload the proteasome pathway; therefore, an initial partial loss of function can eventually lead to a dominant negative gain of function outcome. This notion is consistent with the progressive nature of ALS.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about disease progression.

claim: Disruption of UBQLN4 or UBA1 function could lead to beta-catenin accumulation and aberrant signaling.
source: Disruption of UBQLN4 or UBA1 function, which are both involved in the UPS pathway, could therefore lead to beta-catenin accumulation and aberrant signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the known roles of these proteins in the UPS and the observed effects on beta-catenin.

claim: Heightened beta-catenin activity is a common mechanism between ALS and SMA.
source: Collectively these studies suggest heightened beta-catenin activity as a common mechanism between the adult-onset motor neuron disease ALS and the pediatric motor neuron disease SMA.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing findings in this study with those from the UBA1/SMA study.

claim: Dysregulation of UBQLN4 function by the ALS-associated UBQLN4D90A variant leads to compromised proteasome function and beta-catenin accumulation.
source: Taken together, we revealed a novel role for UBQLN4 in regulating motor axon morphogenesis through the UPS. Dysregulation of this function by the ALS-associated UBQLN4D90A variant leads to compromised proteasome function and beta-catenin accumulation, conferring abnormalities in motor axon morphogenesis (Figure 5), and contributing to motor neuron degeneration in ALS.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented.

claim: Dysregulation of UBQLN4 function confers abnormalities in motor axon morphogenesis and contributes to motor neuron degeneration in ALS.
source: Dysregulation of this function by the ALS-associated UBQLN4D90A variant leads to compromised proteasome function and beta-catenin accumulation, conferring abnormalities in motor axon morphogenesis (Figure 5), and contributing to motor neuron degeneration in ALS.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data and speculative reasoning about disease pathogenesis.

claim: UBQLN4 has a novel role in regulating motor axon morphogenesis through the UPS.
source: Taken together, we revealed a novel role for UBQLN4 in regulating motor axon morphogenesis through the UPS.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental findings.

claim: Wild-type UBQLN4 associates with beta-catenin through its UBA domain and with the proteasome through its UBL domain to allow degradation of beta-catenin.
source: Wild-type UBQLN4 associates with beta-catenin through its UBA domain, and with the proteasome through its UBL domain. These interactions allow for the degradation of beta-catenin, which in turn modulates gene expression to control motor axon morphogenesis.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5A and inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Beta-catenin degradation modulates gene expression to control motor axon morphogenesis.
source: These interactions allow for the degradation of beta-catenin, which in turn modulates gene expression to control motor axon morphogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and established knowledge about beta-catenin function.

claim: The ALS-associated UBQLN4D90A variant is deficient in mediating proteasomal degradation of beta-catenin.
source: The ALS-associated UBQLN4D90A variant is deficient in mediating proteasomal degradation of beta-catenin, leading to its accumulation and excessive induction of gene expression.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5B and supported by experimental data.

claim: Hyperactivation of beta-catenin-controlled genes dysregulates axon morphogenesis, causing aberrant axon branching in motor neurons.
source: Hyperactivation of beta-catenin-controlled genes dysregulates axon morphogenesis, causing aberrant axon branching in motor neurons.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5B and supported by experimental data showing rescue with beta-catenin inhibition.

claim: UBQLN4 contains a UBL domain spanning amino acids 13-83.
source: Domains include a UBL: ubiquitin-like domain, aa 13–83; four STI1 heat-shock-chaperonin-binding motifs, aa 192–229, 230–261, 393–440 and 444–476; and a UBA: ubiquitin-associated domain, aa 558–597.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B.

claim: UBQLN4 contains four STI1 heat-shock-chaperonin-binding motifs at amino acids 192-229, 230-261, 393-440, and 444-476.
source: Domains include a UBL: ubiquitin-like domain, aa 13–83; four STI1 heat-shock-chaperonin-binding motifs, aa 192–229, 230–261, 393–440 and 444–476; and a UBA: ubiquitin-associated domain, aa 558–597.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B.

claim: UBQLN4 contains a UBA domain spanning amino acids 558-597.
source: Domains include a UBL: ubiquitin-like domain, aa 13–83; four STI1 heat-shock-chaperonin-binding motifs, aa 192–229, 230–261, 393–440 and 444–476; and a UBA: ubiquitin-associated domain, aa 558–597.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B.

claim: The proband (III3) had disease duration of 22 months.
source: The proband (III3, arrow) had disease onset at 55 years of age, with disease duration of 22 months.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: The proband's mother (II3) died of ALS at 62 years of age.
source: Her mother (II3) died of ALS at 62 years of age without clear information regarding disease onset.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: The proband's maternal aunt (II2) developed ALS with disease onset at 51 years of age and disease duration of 36 months.
source: Her maternal aunt (II2) developed ALS with disease onset at 51 years of age, and disease duration of 36 months.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: The proband's cousin (III1) developed ALS at 56 years of age and died five years later.
source: Her cousin (III1) developed ALS at 56 years of age and died five years later.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: The proband's maternal grandfather (I2) died in a traffic accident without any known neurological problems.
source: Her maternal grandfather (I2) died in a traffic accident without any known neurological problems.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.
